Cart
KART
noun
From the Saxon craet, a carriage or waggon, akin to the Welsh cart; a two-wheeled vehicle drawn by beasts for carrying burdens. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew agalah, the waggon of the field and the road.

Biblical Definition

A cart is a wheeled waggon drawn by oxen or kine, used for sheaves, for goods, and for the road. Its doctrinal weight in Scripture comes from one thing: the Philistines put the ark of God upon one. Having been plagued for keeping it, their priests and diviners counselled, “make a new cart, and take two milch kine, on which there hath come no yoke” (1Sa 6:7), and God in mercy let the kine carry it straight to Bethshemesh, for He was pleading His own cause among the heathen who had no law. But Israel had a law. The ark was to be borne upon the shoulders of the Kohathites by staves that were never to be removed (Num 4:15; Exo 25:14–15). When David fetched it up, he copied the Philistine method: “they set the ark of God upon a new cart” (2Sa 6:3), and Uzzah, when the oxen shook it, put forth his hand to steady it, and God smote him there for his error, and there he died by the ark of God (2Sa 6:7). The cart was new, the intention was good, the joy was loud, and a man died. David learned the lesson and stated it plainly before the second attempt: “because ye did it not at the first, the LORD our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order” (1Ch 15:13). The cart is therefore the standing emblem of worship offered by man’s device instead of God’s prescription — sincere, borrowed from the nations, and fatal.

Webster 1828 Definition

A two-wheeled waggon for burdens; in Scripture the vehicle on which the ark was carried contrary to God’s command, and thus the emblem of worship by human invention.

CART, n. [Saxon craet; Welsh cart.] A carriage with two wheels, fitted to be drawn by one horse or by oxen, and used for the carriage of heavy commodities.

In Scripture, the waggon (Hebrew agalah) used for sheaves, goods, and journeys.

The new cart of 1Sa 6:7 and 2Sa 6:3, upon which the ark of God was set.

Cart rope, a strong rope; figuratively, the cords by which men draw iniquity (Isa 5:18).

Proverbially, to set the cart before the horse: to invert the right order of things.

Key Scripture

1Sa 6:7 — "Now therefore make a new cart, and take two milch kine, on which there hath come no yoke, and tie the kine to the cart, and bring their calves home from them:"

2Sa 6:3 — "And they set the ark of God upon a new cart, and brought it out of the house of Abinadab that was in Gibeah: and Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, drave the new cart."

2Sa 6:7 — "And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah; and God smote him there for his error; and there he died by the ark of God."

1Ch 15:13 — "For because ye did it not at the first, the LORD our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order."

Modern Corruption

The new cart is the perpetual argument of the innovator: that God will bless whatever is offered sincerely, newly built, and popular — against which the regulative principle and Uzzah’s grave stand together.

expand to see more

The corruption is old and thoroughly modern at once. It says that in worship, sincerity sanctifies the method; that what God has not commanded He has therefore permitted; that the question to ask of a service is whether it moves people and draws them, not whether He appointed it. Every generation builds a new cart. Rome built one of images, relics, and a sacrifice re-offered; the revivalist built one of the anxious bench and engineered decision; our own age builds one of the produced service, the theatrical set, the drama and the dance, and defends it by results. But the ark was not lacking transport — it was lacking the staves and the shoulders God appointed. Note carefully that the cart was borrowed from Philistia, and that the borrowing was the very thing: Israel took her worship-method from the nations because it looked reverent and worked once. It had worked for the Philistines because God was not dealing with them by covenant law.

Recover the due order. This is the regulative principle of worship stated by David himself in 1Ch 15:13: what the LORD commanded is required, and what He has not commanded is not ours to add, however new the timber. Uzzah’s death is not an overreaction to a small mistake; it is God’s public verdict that His prescribed way is not a suggestion, and it is recorded so that we need not learn it as David did. The second procession went right because the Levites bore the ark upon their shoulders with the staves, as Moses commanded according to the word of the LORD (1Ch 15:15) — and the joy of that day was greater, not less, for being obedient.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The ox-drawn waggon; God’s ark set upon it by man’s device, and the death of Uzzah as the seal upon the due order of worship.

expand to see more

Cart — Saxon craet, a waggon or carriage for burdens.

Hebrew agalah, the waggon of the field, the road, and the Philistine device (1Sa 6:7).

Contrast Num 4:15 and Exo 25:14–15: the ark borne on staves upon Kohathite shoulders.

2Sa 6:3–7 — the new cart, Uzzah’s hand, and the breach at Perezuzzah.

1Ch 15:13–15 — David names the sin (not the due order) and corrects it.

Usage

"A “new cart” in Reformed usage means an unprescribed method of worship, however sincere."

"God’s forbearance toward the Philistines was not a precedent for Israel — they had the law."

"1Ch 15:13 is the clearest Old Testament statement of the regulative principle."
